title: Fact, inference or guess?
goal: Test every statement. Does a sentence say it? Do two clues point to it? Or is it only a guess?

card.title: CAN YOU TAP IT? → FACT. TWO CLUES? → INFERENCE. NEITHER? → GUESS. A JUDGMENT? → OPINION.
lines: FACT: a sentence says it, in these words or in other words. Prove it by tapping the sentence.
INFERENCE: no sentence says it, but two clues in the text point to it.
GUESS: fewer than two clues in the text, clues only from your own head, or the text says the opposite.
OPINION: a judgment, like GOOD, BAD, BEST, UNFAIR or SHOULD. Nobody can prove it.
Not a fact? Look for a judgment word first. A judgment is an OPINION, even when there are no clues.
If it feels obvious, that does not make it a fact. Only a sentence makes it a fact.

inference.label: INFERENCE
inference.test: no sentence says it, but two clues point to it

guess.label: GUESS
guess.test: fewer than two clues in the text, or the text says the opposite

opinion.label: OPINION
opinion.test: a judgment: good, bad, best, boring, unfair, should

feedback.hint1: Read the statement again. Does a sentence say it?
feedback.fingerMissed: Look again. One sentence says this. It may use different words.
feedback.fingerWrong: That sentence does not say this. Keep looking.
feedback.fingerNone: Read that sentence again. Does it SAY this? If not, tap No sentence says it.
feedback.clueWrong: That sentence does not point to it. Look for another clue.
feedback.boxAsk: So which box is it? Look for a judgment word first.

box.inference: Count the clues in the text. At least two point to it.
box.guess: Count the clues in the text. Clues from your own head do not count. Are there two?
box.opinion: Look for a judgment word, like GOOD, BAD, BEST, UNFAIR or SHOULD. A judgment is an OPINION.

levels.description: The clue, the reasoning and the inference are all there, and they link.
Only a label (fact, inference, guess), or nothing usable.

gym.title: Seven Sharp
sentences: Marcus checked his phone for the third time in a minute.
The coach had said seven sharp, and the gym door was still locked.
Two other players sat on the steps, scrolling.
At 7:04 a car pulled in fast and the coach jumped out, keys in hand, a coffee stain down the front of his shirt.
"Sorry, sorry," he said, unlocking the door.
"Nobody mention this to the principal."
Marcus grinned.
Last week the coach had benched him for being three minutes late.

dinner.title: At the Table
sentences: "You're not eating," Dad said.
"I ate at Jamal's," Lena said, pushing the rice around her plate.
"Jamal's mom cooks?"
"Sometimes."
Dad put his fork down.
"Lena. The math test. How did it go?"
She didn't look up.
"They haven't given them back yet."
"That's not what I asked."

drinks.title: No More Energy Drinks
sentences: Riverside High's cafeteria stopped selling energy drinks in September.
The principal, Ms. Okafor, said the decision followed complaints from teachers about students who were "wired in period one and asleep by period four."
Sales of water and juice have gone up since the change.
Some students have started bringing energy drinks from the corner store across the street, and the store's owner says his morning sales have doubled.
A student council survey found that 61 percent of students disagreed with the ban.
Ms. Okafor says the policy will be reviewed in January.

shift.title: First Shift
sentences: Amira got to the grocery store twenty minutes before her first shift.
She read the name tag on her shirt twice to make sure it was spelled right.
A supervisor named Carl showed her how to scan items and where to find the codes for fruit.
"You'll be slow today. Everyone is," he said.
Her first customer had a full cart, and Amira dropped a can of beans on the floor.
Her hands shook as she picked it up.
The customer smiled and said, "Take your time."
For the first hour, the line at her register was the longest in the store.
By the end of the shift, it was as short as the others.
Carl walked past and gave her a thumbs-up.
On the bus home, Amira texted her sister: "I think I can do this."
shift.tutorNote: Amira, Carl and the store are invented.

cart.title: The Breakfast Cart
sentences: Pinecrest High started a free breakfast cart in October.
Every morning, two student volunteers push the cart through the front hall with fruit, granola bars and milk.
Vice-principal Renee Whitlock said the idea came from teachers who noticed students with their heads on their desks before nine o'clock.
In the first month, the cart gave out about 150 items a day.
The granola bars are always gone by 8:20.
Apples are often left over.
Since the cart began, the office has recorded fewer late arrivals to first period.
A parent group paid for the first three months of food.
Ms. Whitlock said the school is now looking for a local business to help pay for the rest of the year.
cart.tutorNote: Pinecrest High and the people in this passage are invented.

sections.title: Four boxes
sections.tutorNote: I DO. Read the four boxes together. Reveal the kitchen example one step at a time, then do the fact-or-opinion sort as a quick refresh. Then reveal the gym example, thinking aloud. Two key ideas: feeling obvious does not make it a fact, only a sentence does; and a judgment word (good, bad, best, unfair, should) makes it an opinion.

text: Any statement about a text goes in one of four boxes.
FACT: a sentence says it, in these words or in other words. You can tap that sentence.
INFERENCE: no sentence says it, but two clues point to it.
GUESS: fewer than two clues, or the clues are from your own head, or the text says the opposite.
OPINION: a judgment, like good, bad, best or unfair. Nobody can prove it.
The trick: if it feels obvious, that does NOT make it a fact. Only a sentence makes it a fact.

reveals.label: What you see
reveals.text: You walk into the kitchen. The frying pan is on the stove and still warm. There is a plate with crumbs. Your brother's backpack is gone from its hook.

reveals.label: FACT
reveals.text: The pan is warm. The backpack is gone. You can see and touch these.

reveals.label: INFERENCE
reveals.text: Your brother ate breakfast and left for school. Nobody told you that. But three clues point to it: the warm pan, the crumbs, the missing backpack.

reveals.label: GUESS
reveals.text: He had eggs. The pan shows he cooked something. Nothing shows it was eggs.

reveals.label: OPINION
reveals.text: He is lazy for not washing the pan. That is a judgment.

steps.prompt: Fact or opinion? Here there is no text, so a fact is something you could check. An opinion is a judgment someone could disagree with.

cards.text: The gym is on Main Street.

cards.why: BEST is a judgment. Someone could disagree.
TERRIBLE is a judgment. Not everyone agrees.

steps.hint2: Ask: could I check this, or is it a judgment?
steps.hint3: Look for a judgment word like BEST, UNFAIR or TERRIBLE.

reveals.label: Statement 1
reveals.text: The gym door was locked.

reveals.label: Finger test
reveals.text: Sentence 3 says 'the gym door was still locked.' I can tap it. FACT.

reveals.label: Statement 2
reveals.text: The coach was in a hurry.

reveals.label: Finger test
reveals.text: No sentence says he was in a hurry, in these words or in other words. It feels obvious, but it is not a fact.

reveals.label: Count the clues
reveals.text: 'Pulled in fast.' 'Jumped out, keys in hand.' 'Sorry, sorry.' The clues are in sentence 5 and sentence 6, and nothing says the opposite. INFERENCE.

reveals.label: Statement 3
reveals.text: The coach overslept.

reveals.label: Count the clues
reveals.text: He was late. But late could be traffic or a flat tire. No clue points to sleeping. GUESS.

sections.title: Test it together
sections.tutorNote: WE DO on the same story. The student runs the finger test aloud for every statement before tapping. For anything that is not a fact: look for a judgment word first, then count clues, and ask whether the clues are in the text or in your head. Two statements can be argued two ways, and the screen accepts both: statement 3 (BEST is a judgment word, so opinion; the paper key says guess) and statement 6 (the paper key says guess; inference if the stain and the fast car are counted as two clues). The fifth screen is a discussion. The last statement shows a guess that the text contradicts.

steps.statement: The coach had a coffee stain on his shirt.
steps.why: The words are 'a coffee stain down the front of his shirt.'
steps.hint2: Search for COFFEE.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 4 or sentence 5.

steps.statement: The coach said "Sorry, sorry" as he unlocked the door.
steps.why: The words are in the story: 'Sorry, sorry,' he said, unlocking the door.
steps.hint2: Search for SORRY.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 6 or sentence 7.

steps.statement: Marcus is the best player on the team.
steps.why: BEST is a judgment word. One person could call Marcus the best player and another could disagree. The story does not say how well he plays.

accept.guess: GUESS can be argued too: nothing in the story says how well Marcus plays. But BEST is a judgment word, so OPINION is the better box.

boxWhy.inference: Which clues in the story show how well Marcus plays? There are none. And look at the word BEST.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word BEST. Is it a judgment?
steps.hint3: It is not an INFERENCE. There are no clues about how he plays.

steps.statement: The coach is a bad coach.
steps.why: BAD is a judgment. One person could call him a bad coach and another could disagree. No sentence could prove who is right.

boxWhy.inference: He was late once. But BAD COACH is a judgment about him, and clues cannot prove a judgment.
boxWhy.guess: It is not in the text, that is true. But BAD is a judgment word. A judgment is an OPINION.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word BAD. Could two people disagree about it?
steps.hint3: It is a GUESS or an OPINION. Is BAD a judgment word?

reveals.label: The statement
reveals.text: Marcus kept checking the time.

reveals.label: Finger test
reveals.text: Sentence 1 says he 'checked his phone for the third time in a minute.' Sentence 2 shows what he saw: 6:58.

reveals.label: Fact or inference?
reveals.text: You can call it a FACT: sentence 1 tells what he did, in other words. Or you can call it an INFERENCE, because the word TIME is not in sentence 1. Then name your two clues.

reveals.label: Tell your tutor
reveals.text: Which box did you pick, and why? Both can be argued. What matters is the proof.

steps.statement: The coach had spilled his coffee on the way to the gym.
steps.why: The stain is there, but the story does not say when or where it happened. One clue is not two, and it does not point to ON THE WAY.

near.why: That sentence says there was a stain. It does not say when or where the coffee spilled.

accept.inference: You can argue INFERENCE if you count the stain and the fast car as two clues. But neither clue says WHEN the coffee spilled, so GUESS is the safer box. Talk about it with your tutor.

boxWhy.opinion: This is about what happened. It is not a judgment. Count the clues in the text.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at sentence 5. What does it say about the coffee, and what does it leave out?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Count the clues that say WHEN the coffee spilled.

steps.statement: Marcus found it funny that the coach was late.
steps.why: The text says Marcus grinned. Last week the coach benched him (made him sit out) for being three minutes late, and now the coach is late himself. People grin when something is funny. So probably Marcus found it funny.

near.why: That sentence shows the coach was late. Which sentences show how MARCUS felt about it?
That is the coach talking. Which sentences show how MARCUS felt?

boxWhy.guess: Look at the last two sentences. What did Marcus do, and what happened to him last week?
boxWhy.opinion: FUNNY is how Marcus felt. It is not a judgment about him. Look for clues.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what Marcus does near the end, and what happened to him last week.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 8 and 9.

steps.statement: The coach got to the gym before seven.
steps.why: The text says the opposite. The coach's car pulled in at 7:04, after seven. When the text says the opposite, the statement is a GUESS, and a wrong one.

near.why: Read it again. The car pulled in at 7:04. That is AFTER seven, so the text says the opposite.
That sentence tells what time the coach SAID. Which sentence shows when he came?

boxWhy.inference: Check for the opposite first. When did the coach's car pull in?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about a time. It is not a judgment. When did the coach's car pull in?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at sentence 5. What time did the car pull in?
steps.hint3: The text says the opposite. Which box is that?

sections.title: Clues in a conversation
sections.tutorNote: WE DO on a short conversation. In a dialogue, feelings are in what people do and in what they do not say. For each inference the student taps two clues. 'Lena failed the test' is the key item: BADLY is supported by clues, FAILED is not. Statement 5 is 'Dad is being unfair to Lena' here (the paper sheet has 'Dad is a strict parent', which a careful reader could also call an inference).

text: In a conversation, people do not always say what they feel.
Look at what they DO, and at what they do NOT answer.
Each one is a clue. Two clues that point the same way make an inference.
One clue, or a clue from your own head, is only a guess.

steps.statement: Lena says she ate at Jamal's.
steps.why: Her words are 'I ate at Jamal's.'
steps.hint2: Search for JAMAL.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 2 or sentence 3.

steps.statement: Lena is upset about something.
steps.why: The text says she is not eating, she pushes her rice around, and she will not look up. People do that when something is bothering them. So probably she is upset.

near.why: That part is about Jamal's mom. It does not show how Lena feels.

boxWhy.guess: Look at what Lena does with her food and with her eyes. Are there two clues?
boxWhy.opinion: UPSET is how Lena feels. It is not a judgment about her. Can you find clues for it?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what Lena does, not at what she says.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. Clues: she is not eating, she pushes the rice around, she does not look up.

steps.statement: Lena thinks the math test went badly.
steps.why: The text says she does not look up, and she answers a different question about the test. People avoid a question when the answer is bad. So probably she thinks it went badly.

near.why: That is Dad's question. Which sentences show how Lena reacts to it?

boxWhy.guess: Look at how Lena answers Dad's question about the test. Does she really answer it?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what Lena thinks. It is not your judgment. Look for clues in what she does.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what happens right after Dad asks about the test.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 7, 8 and 9.

steps.statement: Lena failed the test.
steps.why: The story gives no mark. Lena says the tests are not back. She may think it went badly, but BADLY is not FAILED.

near.why: In that sentence Lena says the tests are not back yet. The story gives no mark.

boxWhy.inference: The clues point to WORRIED. Do any clues point to FAILED? The story gives no mark.
boxWhy.opinion: This is about a mark. It is not a judgment. Does the story give a mark?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Read sentence 8. Does the story give a mark?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Do the clues say FAILED, or only WORRIED?

steps.statement: Dad is being unfair to Lena.
steps.why: UNFAIR is a judgment. One reader could say Dad is being unfair. Another could say he is being a caring parent. No sentence could prove who is right.

boxWhy.inference: He asks about the test twice. But UNFAIR is a judgment about him, and clues cannot prove a judgment.
boxWhy.guess: It is not in the text, that is true. But UNFAIR is a judgment word. A judgment is an OPINION.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word UNFAIR. Could two readers disagree about it?
steps.hint3: It is a GUESS or an OPINION. Is UNFAIR a judgment word?

steps.statement: Dad tells Lena that she has not answered his question.
steps.why: Dad is the one speaking. 'That's not what I asked' says the same thing in different words.

near.why: That is the question. Which sentence tells Lena she has not answered it?

steps.hint2: A fact can be said in different words. Look at Dad's last line.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 6 or sentence 9.

sections.title: Say why
sections.tutorNote: WE DO. An inference has three parts: the clue, the reasoning, and the inference. The student says each frame aloud before typing. The middle step (I know that) is the one that gets skipped; ask 'What do you know about people who do that?' The typed answers go to the review queue; score 0 to 3.

text: An inference has three parts.
THE TEXT SAYS: the clue.
I KNOW THAT: what you already know about people or things like this.
SO PROBABLY: the inference.
The clues must come from the text. What you know only explains them.
Say it out loud first. Then type it.

steps.title: Watch one

reveals.label: The text says
reveals.text: Marcus grinned. Last week the coach benched him (made him sit out) for being three minutes late, and now the coach is late himself.

reveals.label: I know that
reveals.text: people grin when something is funny or feels fair.

reveals.label: So probably
reveals.text: Marcus found it funny.

reveals.label: All three parts
reveals.text: The clue comes from the text. The reasoning is what I know. The inference comes last.

steps.question: Why can we say Marcus found it funny that the coach was late?

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "Lena is upset about something."
model: The text says she pushes her food around and won't look up.
I know that people do that when something is bothering them.
So probably she's upset.

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "Lena thinks the math test went badly."
model: The text says she answers a different question about the test and doesn't look up.
I know that people avoid a question when the answer is bad.
So probably she thinks it went badly.

sections.title: Test it on your own
sections.tutorNote: YOU DO on a new passage: nine statements. Watch which box is confused with which; that pattern decides what to reteach. Three statements are worded a little differently from the paper sheet (3, 6 and 7), so that each has one fair answer when the screen marks it. Statement 9 on the paper sheet (the ban started at the beginning of the school year: one text clue plus what you know) is left out; do it aloud afterwards.

text: Read the text first.
Then test each statement. Tap the sentence that says it, or tap No sentence says it.

steps.statement: The cafeteria no longer sells energy drinks.
steps.why: 'Stopped selling' means the same as 'no longer sells.'
steps.hint2: Search for CAFETERIA.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 1 or sentence 3.

steps.statement: Teachers complained about how students were behaving in class.
steps.why: It says the decision 'followed complaints from teachers' about students who were wired (too full of energy), then asleep.
steps.hint2: Search for TEACHERS.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 2 or sentence 5.

steps.statement: The corner store is selling more because of the ban.
steps.why: The text says the cafeteria stopped selling energy drinks. It also says students now bring them from the corner store, and the store's morning sales have doubled. When one place stops selling something, people buy it somewhere else. So probably the store is selling more because of the ban.

near.why: Water and juice sales went up at the cafeteria. That is not about the corner store.

boxWhy.guess: Look at sentence 1 and sentence 4. What did the cafeteria stop doing, and what happened at the store?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what happened. It is not a judgment. Look for clues in sentences 1 and 4.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. What did the cafeteria stop doing, and what happened at the store after that?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 1 and 4.

steps.statement: The store's owner says his morning sales have doubled.
steps.why: The words are 'the store's owner says his morning sales have doubled.'
steps.hint2: Search for OWNER.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 3 or sentence 4.

steps.statement: Most students support the ban.
steps.why: The text says the opposite: 61 percent of students DISAGREED with the ban. Always check for the opposite before you call something an inference.

near.why: Read it again. 61 percent DISAGREED with the ban. That is the opposite.

boxWhy.inference: Check for the opposite first. What does sentence 5 say most students think?
boxWhy.opinion: This is a claim about what students think, and the survey checked it. What did the survey find?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the survey in sentence 5.
steps.hint3: The text says the opposite. Which box is that?

steps.statement: The ban could change.
steps.why: The text says the policy will be reviewed in January, and 61 percent of students disagreed with it. A review can end in a change. So probably the ban could change.

near.why: That sentence says the policy will be REVIEWED. It does not say it will change. So it is a clue, not a fact.

boxWhy.guess: Look at the last two sentences. What will happen in January, and what do most students think?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what could happen. It is not a judgment. Look for clues.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. What will happen in January?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 5 and 6.

steps.statement: The ban is unfair to students.
steps.why: UNFAIR is a judgment. Most students disagreed with the ban, but that does not prove it is unfair. People can disagree about what is fair.

boxWhy.inference: Most students disagreed with the ban. But UNFAIR is a judgment, and clues cannot prove a judgment.
boxWhy.guess: It is not in the text, that is true. But UNFAIR is a judgment word. A judgment is an OPINION.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word UNFAIR. Could two people disagree about it?
steps.hint3: It is a GUESS or an OPINION. Is UNFAIR a judgment word?

steps.statement: The principal regrets the ban.
steps.why: Nothing in the text shows how Ms. Okafor feels about the ban. A review in January is not regret.

near.why: That sentence says the policy will be reviewed. It does not say how she feels.

boxWhy.inference: She will review the policy. Does that show she REGRETS it? A review is not a feeling.
boxWhy.opinion: REGRETS is about how she feels. It is not a judgment. Are there clues for it in the text?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Find every sentence about Ms. Okafor. Do any show her feelings?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Count the clues about her feelings.

steps.statement: Students who drink energy drinks get lower grades.
steps.why: Sentence 2 says some students were asleep by period four. But the text says nothing about grades. One clue plus your own idea is a GUESS.

boxWhy.inference: Sentence 2 gives one clue: some students were asleep by period four. Nothing is said about grades. One clue plus your own idea is a guess.
boxWhy.opinion: This is a claim about grades. It is not a judgment. Does the text say anything about grades?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Does any sentence talk about grades or marks?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Are there two clues in the text?

sections.title: Explain two inferences
sections.tutorNote: YOU DO. The two inferences from the energy-drinks passage, written in the three-part frame. They go to the review queue; score 0 to 3 (clue, reasoning, inference).

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "The corner store is selling more because of the ban."
model: The text says the cafeteria stopped selling energy drinks, and now students bring them from the corner store, where sales have doubled.
I know that when one place stops selling something, people buy it somewhere else.
So probably the store is selling more because of the ban.

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "The ban could change."
model: The text says the policy will be reviewed in January and 61 percent of students disagreed with it.
I know that a review can end in a change.
So probably the ban could change.

sections.title: Home practice
sections.tutorNote: Home set on a new story: eight statements and one written explanation. Assign after 'Test it on your own'.

text: Read the text first.
Then test each statement. Tap the sentence that says it, or tap No sentence says it.

steps.statement: Amira arrived early for her first shift.
steps.why: 'Twenty minutes before her first shift' means she was early.
steps.hint2: A fact can be said in different words. Look for a time.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 1 or sentence 9.

steps.statement: Amira was nervous when she started.
steps.why: The text says she read her name tag twice, she dropped a can, and her hands shook. People do those things when they are nervous. So probably she was nervous.

near.why: Coming early does not tell you how she felt. Which sentences show how she FELT?

boxWhy.guess: Look at what Amira does with her name tag and with her hands. Are there two clues?
boxWhy.opinion: NERVOUS is how Amira felt. It is not a judgment about her. Look for clues.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what Amira's hands do.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. Clues: the name tag, the dropped can, the shaking hands.

steps.statement: Carl showed Amira how to scan items.
steps.why: The words are 'showed her how to scan items.'
steps.hint2: Search for SCAN.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 3 or sentence 4.

steps.statement: Amira wants to become a store manager.
steps.why: Nothing in the story is about what Amira wants to be. No clues means GUESS.

boxWhy.inference: Which sentence is about what Amira wants to be one day? None. Clues from your own head do not count.
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what Amira wants. It is not a judgment. Does the story say anything about it?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Does any sentence talk about what Amira wants to be?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Count the clues in the text.

steps.statement: Amira got faster as the shift went on.
steps.why: The text says her line was the longest in the store for the first hour, and as short as the others by the end. A line gets shorter when the cashier works faster. So probably she got faster.

near.why: That is what Carl said would happen at the start. Which sentences show what DID happen to her line?
That shows Carl was pleased. Which sentences are about her LINE?

boxWhy.guess: Look at her line in the first hour, and her line at the end. Are there two clues?
boxWhy.opinion: FASTER is something you can see in her line. It is not a judgment. Look for clues.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what the story says about the line at her register.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 8 and 9.

steps.statement: Carl told Amira she would be fast on her first day.
steps.why: The text says the opposite. Carl said, 'You'll be slow today.'

near.why: Read it again. Carl said she would be SLOW today. That is the opposite.

boxWhy.inference: Check for the opposite first. What did Carl say in sentence 4?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what Carl said. It is not a judgment. What did he say in sentence 4?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Find what Carl said to Amira.
steps.hint3: The text says the opposite. Which box is that?

steps.statement: Scanning groceries is boring work.
steps.why: BORING is a judgment about the work. One person finds it boring. Another does not.

boxWhy.inference: The story does not show anyone being bored. And BORING is a judgment, which clues cannot prove.
boxWhy.guess: It is not in the text, that is true. But BORING is a judgment word. A judgment is an OPINION.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word BORING. Could two people disagree about it?
steps.hint3: It is a GUESS or an OPINION. Is BORING a judgment word?

steps.statement: A customer told Amira to take her time.
steps.why: The customer's words are 'Take your time.'
steps.hint2: Search for CUSTOMER.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 5 or sentence 7.

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "Amira was nervous when she started."
model: The text says she read her name tag twice, dropped a can, and her hands shook.
I know that people do those things when they are nervous.
So probably she was nervous when she started.

sections.title: Check
sections.tutorNote: Mastery check on a new passage: ten statements and two written explanations. Guide threshold: eight of ten sorted correctly on the first try, every fact tapped and every inference proven with two clues, on two new passages on two different days (the home set is the other passage), and the three-part frame complete for most of the written explanations done alone (the guide's bar is three of four).

text: Read the text first.
Then test each statement. Tap the sentence that says it, or tap No sentence says it.

steps.statement: The breakfast cart does not cost students anything.
steps.why: 'Free' means it costs nothing.

near.why: That sentence says who paid for the food. Which sentence tells you students do not pay?

steps.hint2: A fact can be said in different words. What word means it costs nothing?
steps.hint3: It is sentence 1 or sentence 8.

steps.statement: Some students were coming to school hungry.
steps.why: Teachers saw students with their heads on their desks, and the cart gives out about 150 items a day. Students who take breakfast at school probably did not eat at home. So probably some came to school hungry.

near.why: That part is about who pays. It does not show that students were hungry.

boxWhy.guess: Why did teachers want a breakfast cart? And how much food does it give out? Count the clues.
boxWhy.opinion: HUNGRY is not a judgment. Look for clues in the text.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at what teachers noticed, and at how much food the cart gives out.
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 3, 4 and 5.

steps.statement: The breakfast cart is going to be cancelled.
steps.why: The school is looking for more money, but nothing says the cart will stop. That is a guess about the future.

near.why: That sentence says the school is LOOKING for help to pay. It does not say the cart will stop.

boxWhy.inference: The school is LOOKING for money. Does any sentence point to the cart being cancelled?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what will happen. It is not a judgment. Does any sentence say the cart will stop?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Read the last sentence. What is the school doing?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Do the clues point to CANCELLED?

steps.statement: Student volunteers push the cart through the front hall.
steps.why: The words are 'two student volunteers push the cart through the front hall.'
steps.hint2: Search for VOLUNTEERS.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 2 or sentence 8.

steps.statement: Every school should have a breakfast cart.
steps.why: SHOULD is a judgment about what is right. People can disagree, and no sentence could prove it.

boxWhy.inference: The cart seems to help at this school. But SHOULD is a judgment, and clues cannot prove a judgment.
boxWhy.guess: It is not in the text, that is true. But SHOULD is a judgment word. A judgment is an OPINION.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Look at the word SHOULD. Could two people disagree?
steps.hint3: It is a GUESS or an OPINION. Is SHOULD a judgment word?

steps.statement: Granola bars are more popular than apples.
steps.why: The text says the granola bars are always gone by 8:20 and apples are often left over. The food that runs out first is the food more people want. So probably granola bars are more popular.

near.why: That sentence lists the food on the cart. Which sentences show what students take?

boxWhy.guess: Look at what happens to the granola bars and to the apples. Are there two clues?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about what students take. It is not a judgment about which food is better. Look for clues.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Which food runs out? Which food is left?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 5 and 6.

steps.statement: Apples are the first food to run out.
steps.why: The text says the opposite: apples are often left over.

near.why: Read it again. Apples are often LEFT OVER. That is the opposite.

boxWhy.inference: Check for the opposite first. What does sentence 6 say about apples?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about which food runs out. It is not a judgment. What does sentence 6 say?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Find the sentence about apples. What does it say?
steps.hint3: The text says the opposite. Which box is that?

steps.statement: Fewer students have been late for first period since the cart started.
steps.why: It says the office 'has recorded fewer late arrivals to first period.'
steps.hint2: Search for LATE.
steps.hint3: It is sentence 5 or sentence 7.

steps.statement: Most students at Pinecrest skip lunch.
steps.why: The text is about breakfast. Nothing in it is about lunch.

boxWhy.inference: Which sentence talks about lunch? None. Clues from your own head do not count.
boxWhy.opinion: This is a claim about lunch. It is not a judgment. Does the text say anything about lunch?

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Does any sentence talk about lunch?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE or a GUESS. Are the clues in the text?

steps.statement: The cart does not have enough money yet for the whole year.
steps.why: A parent group paid for three months. The school is looking for a business to pay for the rest. So probably the cart is not paid for all year.

near.why: That sentence says the school is LOOKING for help to pay. It does not say how much money the cart has. It is a clue.

boxWhy.guess: Look at the last two sentences. Who paid, for how long, and what is the school looking for now?
boxWhy.opinion: This is about money. It is not a judgment. Look for clues in the last two sentences.

steps.hint2: No sentence says it. Who paid for the food, and for how long?
steps.hint3: It is an INFERENCE. The clues are in sentences 8 and 9.

steps.prompt: Say it out loud first, then type it.
steps.stem: Explain this inference: "Granola bars are more popular than apples."
model: The text says the granola bars are always gone by 8:20 and apples are often left over.
I know that the food that runs out first is the food more people want.
So probably granola bars are more popular than apples.
